purpose: Ixekizumab is used to treat moderate to severe plaque psoriasis, which causes red, scaly patches on the skin. It is also used for psoriatic arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, and non-radiographic axial spondyloarthritis. Essentially, it helps calm down skin and joint inflammation caused by an overactive immune system.
how_it_works: Your immune system makes a protein called IL-17A that, when overproduced, causes the inflammation behind psoriasis and related conditions. Ixekizumab is like a targeted blocker that attaches to that protein and stops it from triggering inflammation. Think of it as turning down the volume on a specific part of your immune system that is causing the problem.
common_side_effects: The most common side effects include injection site reactions like redness, pain, or swelling where you give the shot. You may also notice upper respiratory infections like the common cold, nausea, or fungal infections such as thrush in the mouth. Some people experience mild redness or bruising at the injection site.
warnings: Because this medication affects your immune system, it can make it harder for your body to fight infections, so tell your doctor right away if you develop signs of infection like fever, chills, or unusual tiredness. You should be tested for tuberculosis before starting this medication. Avoid live vaccines while on this medication. Also let your doctor know if you have inflammatory bowel disease, as it may worsen symptoms in some patients. Do not use if you are allergic to ixekizumab or any of its ingredients.
typical_dosing: For plaque psoriasis in adults, the usual starting dose is 160 mg (two injections of 80 mg) given under the skin, followed by 80 mg every 2 weeks for the first 12 weeks, then 80 mg once a month. Dosing may vary depending on your specific condition, so always follow your doctor's instructions. It comes as a prefilled pen or syringe that you can self-inject at home after proper training.
